blocks: Person/Brian Kernighan and Person/Rob Pike in The UNIX Programming Environment (1984) and Program Design in the UNIX Environment (1984) describe Unix strength as relationships among programs—many utilities are trivial alone but general in combination—and they caution against option sprawl and Swiss-army-knife commands.

Person/Eric S. Raymond in The Art of Unix Programming (2003) collects practical rules (modularity, readability, composition, separate mechanism from policy, small transparent programs, sensible failure modes, favor developer time, prototype before polish, and more).

Person/Mike Gancarz in The UNIX Philosophy (1994) lists nine DEC-era tenets (e.g., small is beautiful, prototype quickly, prefer portability, store data in flat text, use shell scripts and filters, avoid captive user interfaces).
Person/Richard P. Gabriel argues “worse is better”—simplicity of interface and implementation can outcompete correctness-on-paper in the market of ideas that shaped Unix adoption.
Person/Don Norman (1981, Datamation) criticized Unix for poor end-user cognitive ergonomics relative to cognitive-engineering ideals.
Person/Patrick Volkerding cited DOTADIW when arguing that one mega-daemon supervising everything conflicts with classical Unix decomposition.
Person/Jonathan Blow (On the Metal) argued chained small tools can be inefficient without holistic design—drawing parallels to microservices-style coordination costs.

Is there a command like more that is the opposite of less?
Short answer: yes — more itself. It's not really the "opposite" of less, though; it's the older, simpler pager that less was written to replace.
Is there a command like more that is the opposite of less?
more shipped first, in 3BSD (1978). It pages forward through text one screen at a time and, in its original form, can't scroll backward.
Is there a command like more that is the opposite of less?

less came later (Mark Nudelman, 1983-85) as a more capable pager: backward scrolling, search, and the ability to start before the whole input has loaded. Its name is a pun on "less is more" — less does more than more, hence the joke.
Is there a command like more that is the opposite of less?

So there's no separate command that's the naming "opposite" of less — more already is, and it predates less. On most modern systems (Linux, macOS) the more binary is a distinct, more limited implementation from less, not just an alias for it.

Bonus in the same joke lineage: most, a pager written to do even more than less (multi-file, multi-window, wider horizontal scrolling support).

What is a named pipe in Unix, and how do 1Password/Environments use one to mount a .env?

Short answer: a named pipe (a FIFO) is a Unix/Pipe that has a path in the filesystem. It stores nothing; bytes written into one end are handed straight to whoever is reading the other end. 1Password puts a FIFO at your .env path, so when a program opens that "file," the 1Password app writes the secrets into the pipe at that moment and nothing lands on disk.

An ordinary pipe (a | b) is an anonymous kernel buffer between two processes the shell started together. A named pipe is the same buffer given a name in a directory, so unrelated processes can find it by path.

Create one with mkfifo path. ls -l shows file type p, and the size is always 0, because the data only exists in the kernel buffer while it is in transit.

A reader that opens the FIFO blocks until a writer opens it too, and the reverse. Each byte is read once; after one reader consumes it, it is gone.
